W1-1.note: Vesna lifts out the narrator's sweet reed and fits a plainer one, saying a beginner has to hear her own mistakes.

W2-1.note: Vane's plan, which carried 5-2, was to cut a second entrance through the sand spit at Low Point.

W2-2.note: Kerr argued that the district office had made the same undertaking to two other towns and honored it in neither.

W2-3.note: The passage says the Army engineer's dollar-for-dollar letter, not Vane's figures, moved Pell and Danforth.

W2-4.note: The passage covers the vote for the new entrance carried by the federal match, and the cut left at nine feet of a planned fifteen.

W3-1.note: She had still not answered the library when the slips left for the capital, and nothing reached the library.

W3-2.note: The last line names indignation on her behalf at a theft nobody has yet called one; the essayist explicitly rejects comedy, waste and impatience.

W3-3.note: She stood at the market certain that people speak most truly while haggling; C and D reverse her stated rules.

W3-4.note: In 'the old name for a measure of oil', measure means a fixed quantity.

W3-5.note: The paragraph sets out her market-day questioning of sellers and her reasons for refusing written records, children's letters and correspondents.

W3-6.note: Her entries ended up in the capital compiler's dictionary under his name, with her name appearing nowhere, not even among the thanks.

W4-1.note: Paragraph two explains that every other proposed use hit the same wall: the mortgage had to be paid in September.

W4-2.note: Teodor sold Marisol and signed the cheque over to the bank because he would not let the debt shut the yard.

W4-3.note: 'The sale drew half the lake to the shed' means it attracted a crowd.

W4-4.note: She says she was angry all evening and knew even then that the anger was unfair.

W4-5.note: The marina sent a cheque, and on Friday he signed it over to the bank.

W4-6.note: He said the yard outlasts any boat and would not shut its doors to keep one hull, so the debt was his concern.

W5-1.note: The reviewer writes that if the old tempo were restored, the evening would collapse.

W5-2.note: 'The score was recopied from the 1961 parts' refers to written music; the other senses are only played on elsewhere in the paragraph.

W5-3.note: The reviewer says the tempo, taken a third slower, is the one change that does the work.

W5-4.note: 'It is the tempo'; the paragraph then shows each of the other credited changes did not actually happen.

W5-5.note: 'I have nothing to qualify', and he denies worry, any rescue, and fashion as an explanation.

W6-1.note: The soil below the culvert tests four times saltier, the failures cluster in that band, and the other causes are ruled out.

W6-2.note: The writer calls the work good but would take care carrying it beyond this ridge and will not praise it without hedging.

W6-3.note: 'Flush the salt out and the shoots return.'

W6-4.note: In 'a cold spring runs below the boundary rock' run means water flowing; the paragraph explicitly denies the other senses.

W6-5.note: The evidence points to road salt, and every other cause is dismissed.

W7-1.note: 'The club's conduct puzzles me', and the author explicitly denies praise, anger, hope and indifference.

W7-2.note: The surveys point to the dam trapping the silt the nymphs need.

W7-3.note: The catch book dates the last big hatch to June 2010 and records no change in the fishing.

W7-4.note: 'A spring feeds the north bay' and the passage glosses it as a source of cold water.

W7-5.note: 'Return depends on passing silt below the dam', and the other remedies are said to gain nothing.

W7-6.note: 'The surveys point to the dam': silt has not passed it since 2009.
